) and adds one response to surprise to the action rule. After a surprising outcome, the next allocation of nets is wider, and the widening decays over the following trials. The belief update, and therefore the meaning of the six Nexus parameters, is unchanged. The variant describes participants who spread their nets after surprising attacks without changing their belief. It is fitted to all participants as a second description, and its additional parameter is related to the questionnaire scores. It is not part of the model comparison.

children.value: The six Nexus parameters are recovered as in the adopted network. The spread gain is recovered with r = .66. Its rank histogram lies within the 99 % range of a uniform histogram (bin counts 40 to 63, expected 50). In 92.9 % of the calibration simulations, the true gain lies within the central 90 % interval of a normal approximation to the posterior.
Recovery of the gain depends on precision weighting, because a widening of a flat allocation leaves no trace:

Below a precision weighting of 1, the posterior mean of the gain stays at the prior mean of 1 (panel A). In the fit of the participants, one participant has a posterior mean of the precision weighting below 1, and 39 of 96 below 2.

All 96 participants of run 23_11 were fitted, with 4000 posterior draws per participant. The six Nexus parameters agree closely with the adopted fit: Spearman ρ = .80 for noise reactivity and between .91 and .98 for the other five parameters. The median ratio of the posterior SD of the gain to its prior SD is .49.
The posterior mean of the spread gain has a median of .87 (IQR .22–1.39). It differs between the instruction conditions (Kruskal–Wallis H = 11.2, p = .004; a single test):

Within the variant, the gain correlates with noise reactivity (ρ = .54) and belief momentum (ρ = .58), weakly with placement noise (ρ = .23) and negatively with cue sensitivity (ρ = −.27). It is unrelated to precision weighting (ρ = .11) and the switch probability (ρ = .19).
Agreement with the behavioural lag slopes.

The spread variant has more participants inside the interval than the adopted fit on 33 statistics and fewer on 19. The largest differences:
SD of the net entropy across trials: .10 → .19 inside; median |z| 7.65 → 4.33.
Mean circular variance of the placement: .64 → .75.
Mean number of slots with nets: .74 → .82.
Peak of the net entropy after a transition: .73 → .56; median |z| 1.13 → 1.63.
Recovery of the net entropy after a transition: .75 → .64.
Shift of the placement after an oddball: .57 → .49.

For each statistic, the participants who lie inside the interval under only one of the two fits were compared with an exact binomial test (one test per statistic, without correction). In favour of the variant:
mean angular error: 20 against 3 participants, p < .001;
cue difference in net entropy: 21 against 2, p < .001;
SD of the angular error: 11 against 1, p = .006;
In favour of the adopted fit:
peak of the net entropy after a transition: 25 against 9, p = .009;
recovery of the net entropy after a transition: 17 against 6, p = .035.
The SD of the net entropy (11 against 3, p = .057) and the circular variance (19 against 8, p = .052) improve in the same direction.
The widening improves the variability of the allocation across trials and the angular error. It also produces wider allocations after transitions than the participants show.
